# Bedbugs

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Parasitic infections > Bedbugs*

[Original Article Link](/library/C80qK3)

---

## Summary

Bedbugs are <u>ectoparasitic</u> <u>arthropods</u> of the Cimicidae family that feed on blood and are primarily transmitted via direct contact with infested beds or other furniture. They typically hide during the day and venture out for a blood meal at night. Symptoms of <u>bedbug dermatitis</u> include painless hemorrhagic punctum at the sites of the bites, typically followed by pruritic 2–5 mm <u>erythematous</u> <u>maculopapular</u> lesions within hours to days. The diagnosis is confirmed based on the appearance of the lesions and signs of bedbug <u>infestation</u> (e.g., exoskeletons) in the patient's environment. Management focuses on symptomatic treatment of <u>pruritus</u> and decontamination of all furniture and textiles. Complications include secondary infections (e.g., <u>folliculitis</u>) and psychological effects (e.g., <u>anxiety</u> and <u>hypervigilance</u>).

---

## Etiology

* Pathogens: <u>ectoparasitic</u> <u>arthropods</u> of the Cimicidae family [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)

* <u>Cimex lectularius</u> (common bedbug)

* Cimex hemipterus (tropical bedbug)

* Transmission: direct contact with infested beds and other furniture and/or travelers who bring home bedbugs or their eggs (e.g., on clothes, in luggage) from stays in infested residences

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Crowded living conditions

* Travel to a location with an <u>infestation</u>





> [!TIP]
> Bedbug <u>infestations</u> occur worldwide, primarily in temperate and tropical regions. [[3]](/library/X9W9Nn0)

---

## Clinical features

<u>Bedbug dermatitis</u> can be hard to differentiate from other <u>skin</u> conditions and reactions to other <u>arthropod</u> bites. [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)[[4]](/library/EwW8kn0)




* Bedbug dermatitis [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)[[4]](/library/EwW8kn0)

* Location and pattern of bites

* Most commonly on <u>skin</u> regions that are typically uncovered during <u>sleep</u> (e.g., neck, face, arms, hands)

* Often clustered and/or in linear pattern, i.e., “breakfast, lunch, and dinner” pattern    [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)

* Appearance

* Painless hemorrhagic punctum may initially be visible at the sites of the bedbug bites.

* Bites typically develop into 2–5 mm <u>erythematous</u> <u>maculopapular</u> lesions (often pruritic)   within hours or days.  [[3]](/library/X9W9Nn0)

* <u>Wheals</u>, <u>vesicular lesions</u>, or, less commonly, <u>bullae</u> or cutaneous <u>nodules</u> may be present. [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)[[4]](/library/EwW8kn0)

* Duration: spontaneous resolution within 1–2 weeks [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)[[3]](/library/X9W9Nn0)

* Associated symptoms: psychological <u>distress</u>, e.g., <u>sleep deprivation</u>, <u>hypervigilance</u> [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)





> [!TIP]
> Bedbug bites are painless. <u>Bedbug dermatitis</u>, a local cutaneous inflammatory reaction, develops over hours to days. [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)[[4]](/library/EwW8kn0)

---

## Diagnosis

* Suspect <u>bedbug dermatitis</u> based on <u>risk factors</u> and the appearance of the lesions. [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)[[4]](/library/EwW8kn0)

* Confirm the diagnosis based on clear signs of bedbug <u>infestation</u> in the patient's environment, e.g.:

* Bedbugs in various stages of development

* Exoskeletons

* Feces

* The patient or another layperson can inspect the environment, but a pest control service may be necessary.  [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)[[4]](/library/EwW8kn0)

* Traps may aid detection. [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)

---

## Management

### <u>Bedbug dermatitis</u> management [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)




Management is supportive.  [[4]](/library/EwW8kn0)




* Advise patient to wash lesions with soap and <u>antiseptic</u> solution. [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)

* Treat <u>pruritus</u> as needed, e.g., using: [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)

* <u>Topical corticosteroids</u>, e.g., <u>hydrocortisone</u> 1% DOSAGE

* <u>Antihistamines</u>

* Prescribe topical or systemic <u>antibiotic therapy</u> in the event of secondary bacterial infection, e.g., <u>purulent SSTI</u>. [[3]](/library/X9W9Nn0)





> [!TIP]
> Treat cohabitants with similar symptoms if necessary.




### Eradication of <u>infestation</u> [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)




* Heat treatment, e.g., washing, steaming, and use of heating tents [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)[[4]](/library/EwW8kn0)
* Bedbugs are killed:

* Within 1 minute at temperatures â¥ 140Â°F

* Within 2 hours at temperatures â¥ 120Â°F

* Cold treatment

* <u>Freezing</u> at â¤ -4Â°F for at least 2 hours [[2]](/library/rwWf4n0)

* <u>Freezing</u> at â¤ 23Â°F for at least 5 days [[4]](/library/EwW8kn0)

* Physical removal

* Vacuuming with a sealable vacuum bag

* Brushing and cleaning surfaces and luggage to remove eggs

* Insecticides, e.g. pyrethroids, are often ineffective due to widespread bedbug resistance.





> [!TIP]
> Professional extermination is often necessary as part of an integrated pest management strategy.” [[4]](/library/EwW8kn0)
